main.title: Dragon Quest VI
main.subtitle: Recognizing yourself between two worlds
main.summary: On December 9, 1995, Dragon Quest VI: Maboroshi no Daichi was released in Japan for Super Famicom.

cards.heading: Recognizing yourself between two worlds
cards.text: Dragon Quest VI: Maboroshi no Daichi was released in Japan for Super Famicom on December 9, 1995. Its adventure moves between two overlapping worlds, connecting the mysteries of identity with the relationship between reality and dreams. Players compare places and follow clues across both maps. A returning vocation system also lets the party learn abilities through different classes.

cards.heading: Two maps teach you to look twice
cards.text: The two worlds share names and familiar forms but differ in important details. A place visited in one can supply a clue to another, encouraging players to remember locations and return with new knowledge. Square Enix describes discovery as the game's theme. Exploring its geography means gradually understanding how these related places fit together.

cards.heading: Vocations turn growth into a path
cards.text: Choosing a vocation changes a character's statistics, priorities and available abilities. Skills learned along an earlier path remain useful after a class change, giving players room to experiment and plan specialisations. Battles develop both the party's immediate strength and its longer-term repertoire, so a character's growth depends on several choices made over time.

cards.heading: The search for identity runs through the system
cards.text: Square Enix also identifies a search for oneself within the story. Characters travel between realities and uncover relationships that initially seem incomplete or uncertain. Their progress through the worlds gradually clarifies who they are and how they are connected. Alongside that narrative, different vocations allow the same party members to take on changing roles in combat.

main.title: Tales of Phantasia
main.summary: Tales of Phantasia is an action role-playing video game developed by Wolf Team and published by Namco for the Super Famicom.

cards.heading: The first Tales and its later editions
cards.text: Tales of Phantasia was developed by Wolf Team and published by Namco for Japan's Super Famicom in December 1995. The first Tales game later reached PlayStation in 1998 and Game Boy Advance in 2003. Nintendo published the GBA version in North America and Europe in March 2006, marking its first official English release. A Full Voice Edition followed for PSP that September, adding voiced story scenes. Fans had already translated the original Super Famicom game in 2001.

cards.heading: A journey across time
cards.text: The game takes place in a fantasy world of Aselia and follows Cress Albane, a highly-trained swordsman who is driven by vengeance after his hometown is destroyed. Seeking further answers, he finds out that this is none other than a scheme to free the war-mongering Dhaos, the game's main antagonist. To prevent further catastrophes, Cress is aided by the use of time travel to gather allies from the past who can help him put an end to Dhaos's rampage in his own time.

cards.heading: Creators and character design
cards.text: The game was written and programmed by Yoshiharu Gotanda, designed by Masaki Norimoto, and scored by Motoi Sakuraba, Shinji Tamura and Ryota Furuya. The character designs were created by manga artist Kōsuke Fujishima. A short anime series based on the game, called Tales of Phantasia: The Animation, was released in 2004.

cards.heading: Battles, voices and a late Super Famicom release
cards.text: Tales of Phantasia experienced several delays and development challenges prior to its release in 1995, near the end of the Super Famicom's lifespan. It attracted attention due to its graphics, its original battle system, and its use of voice acting. It is also the first and only Super Famicom game to include an original, vocalized theme song. It sold over 1.3 million units in Japan alone, making it the second bestselling game in the franchise in that region, and one of the bestselling games in the franchise as a whole.

main.title: Suikoden
main.subtitle: A revolution needs many people
main.summary: On December 15, 1995, Konami released Suikoden for PlayStation in Japan, beginning a series loosely inspired by the Chinese classic Shui Hu Zhuan, also known as Water Margin.

cards.heading: Gathering a rebellion
cards.text: Konami released Suikoden in Japan for PlayStation on December 15, 1995. Loosely inspired by the Chinese classic Water Margin, it follows a rebellion built around the recruitment of 108 Stars of Destiny. Some join the fighting party; others establish shops and services at its base. Party battles, duels and clashes between armies show the growing conflict from different perspectives.

cards.heading: The 108 Stars of Destiny
cards.text: The 108 Stars of Destiny include people with different skills and roles. Recruiting a warrior expands the party, while another character may open a service or activity at headquarters. Finding these people changes what the rebellion can do and how its home looks. Konami retained recruitment as one of the series' distinctive features, alongside Runes and large-scale battles.

cards.heading: A fortress fills with people
cards.text: As recruits arrive, the Liberation Army's initially empty fortress gains shops, services and activities. The player can walk through the base and meet people who remain there even when they are outside the active party. Its changing rooms give recruitment a visible result, making the headquarters a place to revisit as the rebellion grows.

cards.heading: From a duel to an army
cards.text: Ordinary party combat brings six characters into formation, while duels focus on reading a single opponent. Army Battles shift attention to the forces available to the rebellion. Moving between these forms gives different events their own scale: a personal confrontation, a small group's encounter or a clash involving the movement the protagonist has helped assemble.

main.title: Eidos Interactive
main.subtitle: A British publisher in the 3D era
main.summary: On May 31, 1996 Domark became Eidos Interactive as part of a reorganization bringing together British publishing and development businesses.

cards.heading: Domark becomes Eidos Interactive
cards.text: Domark became Eidos Interactive on May 31, 1996, in a reorganisation joining British publishing and development businesses. The new identity arrived as PlayStation and three-dimensional games were expanding the market. Eidos would publish Tomb Raider, Championship Manager, Deus Ex, Thief and Legacy of Kain, working with studios whose games had markedly different styles.

cards.heading: A larger publishing network
cards.text: The combined business brought publishing, development and video-technology expertise into a larger organisation. Three-dimensional production demanded growing budgets, while console releases required international distribution and promotion. Eidos supplied a commercial network through which studios could bring their projects to audiences in several countries and on different platforms.

cards.heading: The success of Tomb Raider
cards.text: Tomb Raider gave Eidos an internationally recognisable character. Lara Croft appeared in magazines, advertising and campaigns beyond the usual games press, while Core Design developed sequels at a rapid pace. The series became an important part of the publisher's business, placing its commercial schedules alongside the development team's need for production time.

cards.heading: Different studios, different games
cards.text: Thief built its action around stealth and simulated spaces; Deus Ex combined systems, dialogue and player choices; Championship Manager centred on data and management. Eidos published each within the same catalogue, providing distribution and promotion for projects with different design priorities. This range became a defining part of its publishing identity.

main.title: Tomb Raider
main.subtitle: Archaeology by movement
main.summary: Core Design turned the reading of a room into a sequence of measured jumps, climbs and discoveries.

cards.heading: Reading a route through the ruins
cards.text: Tomb Raider's three-dimensional ruins asked players to look for a route before moving. Lara Croft's actions and the architecture shared a consistent scale, making a ledge or gap something the player could learn to judge.

cards.heading: A character beyond the game
cards.text: Lara Croft also became a widely circulated media image through the game's promotion. Her movement system, the work of Core Design's team and the marketing surrounding the character all contributed to Tomb Raider's recognition beyond the game itself.

cards.heading: Creating Lara Croft
cards.text: The initial concept was created by Toby Gard, who is credited as Lara's creator and worked as lead artist on the project. Production began in 1994 and took 18 months, with a budget of £440,000. The character of Lara was based on several influences, including Tank Girl, Indiana Jones, and Hard Boiled. The 3D grid-based level design, innovative for its time, was inspired by the structure of Egyptian tombs. The music was composed by Nathan McCree, who took inspiration from English classical music. Originally announced in 1995, the title went on to receive extensive press attention and heavy promotion from Eidos Interactive. An expansion pack subtitled Unfinished Business was released in 1998, containing new standalone levels.

cards.heading: Making 3D exploration work
cards.text: The development team took several months to find a way to make Gard's vision for the game work on the hardware of the time, in particular getting the player character to interact with freeform environments. Tomb Raider used a custom-built game engine, as did many games of the era. The engine was designed and built by Douglas with assistance from Rummery. Rummery created the level editor, which allowed for "seamless" creation of levels. According to Rummery, the decision to build the game levels on a grid was the key breakthrough in making the game possible. It is Core Design's contention that, prior to the development of Tomb Raider, they were "struggling somewhat" with 32-bit development. Lara's movements were hand-animated and coordinated rather than created using motion capture. The reason for this was that the team wanted uniformity in her movement, which was not possible with motion capture technology of the time.

cards.heading: The sound of silence
cards.text: Unlike most other games of the time, there was not a musical track playing constantly throughout the game; instead, limited musical cues would play only during specially-selected moments to produce a dramatic effect. For the majority of the game, the only audio heard is action-based effects, atmospheric sounds, and Lara's own grunts and sighs, all of which were enhanced because they did not have to compete with music. According to McCree, the game was scored this way because he was allotted very little time for the job, forcing him to quickly write pieces without any thought to where they would go in the game. When the soundtrack was finally applied, the developers found that the tunes worked best when applied to specific places. The symphonic sounds were created using Roland Corporation's Orchestral Expansion board for their JV series keyboards.

main.title: Civilization II
main.summary: Sid Meier's Civilization II is a turn-based strategy video game in the Civilization series, developed and published by MicroProse.

cards.heading: A new Civilization for the PC
cards.text: Sid Meier's Civilization II is a turn-based strategy video game in the Civilization series, developed and published by MicroProse. It was released in 1996 for PCs, and later ported to the PlayStation by Activision.

cards.heading: Conquest or a journey to space
cards.text: Players build a civilization from a primitive tribe, competing with rival computer- or human (in some editions)-controlled civilizations. They manage cities and units in a quest to assure their civilization's dominance—either by conquering all other civilizations or by manufacturing advanced space technology.

cards.heading: Sales and recognition
cards.text: Civilization II was a commercial hit, with sales of around three million units by 2001, and has won numerous awards and placements on "best games of all time" lists. It was followed by Civilization III.

cards.heading: Choosing a civilization
cards.text: As a turn-based strategy game, Civilization II models the historical development of human civilization. A player, when creating a game, may pick one of 21 historical civilizations or a custom-named civilization. The computer will intelligently control multiple rival civilizations. Only a single-player mode was available until the release of the Multiplayer Addon.

cards.heading: Twenty-one peoples on the map
cards.text: The following civilizations appear in the game: Americans, Aztecs, Babylonians, Carthaginians, Celts, Chinese, Egyptians, English, French, Germans, Greeks, Indians, Japanese, Mongols, Persians, Romans, Russians, Sioux, Spaniards, Vikings and Zulus. Barbarians are available as NPCs.

cards.heading: Exploring from 4000 BC
cards.text: The game takes place on a map made of tiles. A human player may generate a random map based on their specifications, or opt for a pre-made map. Different terrain types, special resources and improvements such as irrigation are present on different tiles. Players begin with one or a few units, including settlers to found their first cities, in 4000 BC. All of the map is unexplored except the starting units' immediate vicinity, and exploration is a top early-game priority.

cards.heading: Cities, resources and specialised units
cards.text: Cities occupy one tile and harvest yields from nearby tiles: food, trade and production. They may build units, city improvements or wonders of the world. Typically, each civilization will constantly expand by founding new cities until all of the map is settled. Analogous to chess pieces, the many different units vary in their functions, mirroring historical types of soldiers and occupations. Units occupy one tile at a time and may move every turn. Most of them can attack others in battle; a minority have non-military functions.

main.title: Guardian Heroes
main.summary: Guardian Heroes is a 1996 beat 'em up action role-playing video game developed by Treasure and published by Sega for the Sega Saturn video game console.

cards.text: Guardian Heroes is a 1996 beat 'em up action role-playing video game developed by Treasure and published by Sega for the Sega Saturn video game console. The game resembles other beat 'em ups such as Final Fight or Golden Axe, but with action role-playing elements. The development team called it a "fighting RPG".

The game allows players to alter the storyline through their actions, such as choosing between a number of branching paths, leading to multiple endings, and killing civilians and enemies, leading to changes in the Karma meter. The music was composed by Nazo² Suzuki and Norio Hanzawa. Hideki Matsutake, a former member of electronic music band Yellow Magic Orchestra, is credited as playing the synthesizer for the score. It is considered a cult classic of the beat 'em up genre. A sequel was released in 2004 for the Game Boy Advance entitled Advance Guardian Heroes. A remastered version of Guardian Heroes was released for the Xbox 360 in 2011.

main.title: Neo Turf Masters
main.subtitle: Golf at an arcade pace
main.summary: Neo Turf Masters is Nazca's golf game, first released for Neo Geo arcades on 29 January 1996.

cards.heading: Golf at an arcade pace
cards.text: Neo Turf Masters is Nazca's golf game, first released for Neo Geo arcades on 29 January 1996. Known in Japan as Big Tournament Golf, it offers six golfers and four fictional courses associated with the United States, Japan, Australia and Germany. The presentation gives each shot a quick, clear sequence rather than a lengthy simulation. Stroke play supports one or two players, while match play provides a direct two-player contest. Nazca released it shortly before Metal Slug, showing another side of the studio's ability to make arcade action immediately approachable.

cards.heading: Power, height and the wind
cards.text: The shot system separates power from height. One input sets the strength of the swing, and another determines how high the ball will travel, while hook and slice are selected beforehand. That arrangement makes the controls quick to learn, leaving the course and wind to provide much of the difficulty. A promising line can become unreliable when the conditions change. The player must connect the visible landing area with the chosen club, trajectory and wind, then carry out the short timing sequence that turns the plan into a shot.

cards.heading: Choosing the golfer and the course
cards.text: The golfers' differing attributes give another choice before the round begins, while the four courses vary the situations those strengths must address. Hazards and demanding layouts keep a simple swing system from making the competition predictable. Takushi Hiyamuta composed the music, contributing to its bright arcade atmosphere. Later releases often used the Japanese title Big Tournament Golf. The original's appeal lies in how quickly it reaches the meaningful part of the sport: assess the next stretch of ground, judge the conditions and see whether a precisely timed swing can deliver the intended result.

main.title: Duke Nukem 3D
main.summary: Duke Nukem 3D is a 1996 first-person shooter game developed by 3D Realms and published by FormGen for MS-DOS.

cards.heading: Duke moves into first-person shooting
cards.text: Duke Nukem 3D is a 1996 first-person shooter game developed by 3D Realms and published by FormGen for MS-DOS. It is a sequel to the platform games Duke Nukem and Duke Nukem II, published by 3D Realms.

cards.heading: An alien invasion, acclaim and controversy
cards.text: Duke Nukem 3D features the adventures of the titular Duke Nukem, voiced by Jon St. John, who fights against an alien invasion on Earth. Along with Wolfenstein 3D, Doom and Quake, Duke Nukem 3D is considered to be responsible for popularizing first-person shooters, and was released to major critical acclaim. Reviewers praised the interactivity of the environments, gameplay, level design, and unique risqué humor, a mix of pop-culture satire and lampooning of over-the-top Hollywood action heroes. However, it also incited controversy due to its violence, erotic elements, and portrayal of women. Since its release, Duke Nukem 3D has been cited as one of the greatest video games ever made.

cards.heading: From shareware to World Tour
cards.text: The shareware version was originally released on January 29, 1996, while the full version of the game was released on April 19, 1996. The Plutonium PAK, an expansion pack which updated the game to version 1.4 and added a fourth eleven-level episode, was released on October 21, 1996. The Atomic Edition, a standalone version of the game that included the content from the Plutonium PAK and updated the game to version 1.5, was released on December 11, 1996. A fifth episode was released on October 11, 2016, with 20th Anniversary World Tour published by Gearbox Software. A sequel, Duke Nukem Forever, was released in 2011.

main.title: Bahamut Lagoon
main.subtitle: Square · Super Nintendo Entertainment System
main.summary: Bahamut Lagoon is Square's Super Famicom tactical role-playing game about Byuu and the dragon squad resisting the Granbelos Empire. The world of Orelus consists of lands floating in the sky, giving the campaign a setting of isolated places connected by travel and conflict. Human characters fight in organised squads accompanied by dragons. The player develops both sides of that army, preparing its members between operations before moving them across a grid battlefield where the immediate clash can lead into a closer turn-based encounter.

cards.heading: An army travelling between floating lands
cards.text: Bahamut Lagoon is Square's Super Famicom tactical role-playing game about Byuu and the dragon squad resisting the Granbelos Empire. The world of Orelus consists of lands floating in the sky, giving the campaign a setting of isolated places connected by travel and conflict. Human characters fight in organised squads accompanied by dragons. The player develops both sides of that army, preparing its members between operations before moving them across a grid battlefield where the immediate clash can lead into a closer turn-based encounter.

cards.heading: Feed the dragon for the next battle
cards.text: Weapons, armour and other items can be fed to dragons to change their attributes and eventually their forms. Their preferences affect loyalty, making development involve more than simply offering the strongest spare equipment. During battle, the player gives general instructions while the dragons act with some independence. That separation lets a companion feel like a creature rather than another directly controlled soldier. Preparing its abilities and disposition matters because the next battle will ask it to use those qualities beyond the player's precise control.

cards.heading: A new team finds its own campaign
cards.text: Development began in 1994 with newer Square staff and changed from a conventional role-playing concept into a tactical design. Kazushige Nojima directed, Motomu Toriyama wrote the scenario and Noriko Matsueda composed the score. Designer Hitoshi Sasaki's memories of an aerial view over the Izu Peninsula helped inspire the floating landscape. Released only in Japan in 1996, the game joined intimate party relationships to a larger military campaign, with the dragons providing a second kind of attachment that the player could influence and develop between battles.
